In an earlier comment, @ThomasMakai wrote: "I cannot emphasize enough how important it is to resign sooner rather than later." In my opinion, receiving the "golden call" from Emirates and joining their cabin crew is the result of a tremendous amount of hard work. Hard work involves: 1. Meeting the required English language standards. 2. Developing strong communication skills. 3. Practicing for the assessment day (self-presentation, group activities, English test, final interview). 4. Purchasing the necessary attire for the assessment day. 5. Maintaining the appropriate grooming for the assessment day. 6. Passing the required medical examinations. 7. Gathering the necessary paperwork in English. Achieving the golden call is not just a reward for all the effort invested in the months leading up to it - it's more than that. To me, the golden call represents a second chance in life, an opportunity to start anew in a global mega-city like Dubai, a city full of potential. If someone resigns after three or five years as a cabin crew member, it feels like wasting that incredible opportunity. Emirates cabin crew isn’t just about going to Dubai, living there for a few years, and then returning home. Doing that is like throwing away a golden chance to network, build connections, and grow financially. In my view, receiving the golden call from Emirates is like an initiation—a stepping stone to a new life in Dubai. If I were selected as an Emirates cabin crew member, I would know that Dubai and the UAE would be my home for the rest of my life. Failure is not an option, and neither is resignation. Working for Emirates is a gift. For example, someone could work for Emirates as a cabin crew member for 12 years, and then apply for a role in ground operations, IT, or HR. Twelve years is a significant amount of time - plenty of time to upskill, earn additional certifications, or even pursue a university degree or college diploma. There are also opportunities to branch out into other sectors, such as: 1. Shipping, 2. Real estate. Perhaps someone will even have the chance to start their own business or get involved in the exciting new casino projects coming to the UAE. There’s so much happening in Dubai and the UAE, and I believe resignation is not an option. This golden call is not an opportunity to be missed.

It would certainly be an easy situation to fall into. My experience with flying for forty years with an international carrier was in my home country. Because of that, I was able to have a varied ground life. I was married, had children and attended university all while working as cabin crew. My home town was easily accessible both on work as well as time off travel. This enabled me to remain connected to family and old friends. The part of my life flying was without doubt, the very best imaginable and for all the reasons you stated. After retirement at age 62, I did a teaching diploma and then went to work at a school board for the following 12 years. My advice to cabin crews who are under contract and living in a compound would be to enjoy it to the fullest and leave after 5 or so years but not before having secured another cabin crew job in your home country, preferably being based in your home town. Yo te descubrí cuando hiciste el vídeo con Denisse de las Pochoclo sessions al ser despedida de EK. En ese momento, yo estudiaba derecho y mi sueño era viajar. Estuve dos años viajando y trabajando por Europa, sin terminar la carrera de derecho porque pensaba que esa era la vida que yo quería, los viajes. Hasta que en enero de 2023, terminé la carrera y me uní a EK. Al principio todo era maravilloso, odié el training pero todo lo bueno lo compensaba. A los seis meses, recibí un final warning por algo que me parece estúpido y que se podría haber resuelto hablando las cosas como personas civilizadas. Realmente me afectó, pero todavía quería seguir viajando, hasta que en diciembre fui de vacaciones a España y vi a mi prima. Ella sólo tiene cuatro años más que yo, también es graduada en derecho y tiene un trabajo en estable en un Ayuntamiento donde gana más de lo que yo gano en EK, trabaja muchas menos horas y es feliz junto a su marido y sus hijos. Entonces, sentí como si me cayera un jarro de agua fría. Yo acababa de cumplir veinticinco años, hacía tres años que no tenía nada que ver en el mundo del derecho y estaba "limpiando mierda de indios" a 40.000 pies de altura. En ese momento, deseé tener la vida de mi prima, comencé a pensar que yo valía para algo más que limpiar vómito de indios y empecé a ver a mis compañeras como niñas tontas que no usan su cerebro y sólo hablan de manicura, inyecciones labiales y mejores destinos del mundo. Todavía no tengo claro qué va a ocurrir en mi futuro. Siento que todo lo que me había atraído de este trabajo y el tipo de vida que algún día quise se ha ido a la basura. Ya no quiero los lujos que ofrece Dubái, ni los viajes, ni la vida ajetreada. Soy de un pequeño pueblo en España y siempre desprecié la vida rural y sencilla, y ahora mismo sólo quiero la tranquilidad, poder pasear a mi perrito, dejar de vestirme con blazer para ir a comprar el pan. To the people saying 32k a year is meh: That's for an entry level job that only requires a highschool diploma, speaking English, and some customer service experience (plus the physical stuff like height and overall health). You pay no income tax, no rent, no bills, no transportation to the airport. You also get a per diem in cash whenever you stay out of base (4/6 times a month) which ranges from around $40 to $120, depending on the destination. You get unlimited flights at 90% off. Most crew come from countries where the annual salary doesn't even reach 5k a year. Yeah, Dubai is expensive buy if you live frugally and make the most of the perks (say, buy some of your groceries in a cheaper country when you're on a work trip), you can save a big chunk of your salary. And in comparison, most airlines in Europe pay less than 15k a year. On the flip side, the job is extremely demanding physically and, ultimately, mentally, and the company culture is a whoooooole thing altogether (there's plenty of info online). Also, the flashy events are only for the "business promotion" crew, a select group of pretty people that goes through another selection process. Source: I used to be cabin crew for them. PS: this is all pre-pandemic. I'm absolutely sure the post-pandemic new hires will have much worse contracts.

Both my parents are Emirates Flight Attendants it actually defers on the rank if you are a flight attendant. My dad is the Cabin Supervisor) [CSV] and he supervises the flight attendants and works at Economy and First Class or Business Class. The rank named Grade 1 [G1] works at the Business Class. The rank called Grade 2 [G2] works at the Economy Class. The Grade 1 is a higher rank than Grade 2 for some reason. And the FG1 rank, works at the First Class Section. While the highest rank of all flight attendants which is a purser, supervises the cabin crew too, and works at first class. Here is the list of the ranks in order: Highest: Purser (supervises everyone, works at First Class section). 2nd: Cabin Supervisor ( Serves both Economy and business and supervises the crew). 3rd : FG1 (serves First Class) 4th: Grade 1 (serves Business Class) 5th: Grade 2 (serves Economy Class)
